podcast.title: Acquisition of Global Copyright
podcast.body: Folkways, seeking global rights, secured an agreement with Gallo Records that proved highly disadvantageous to Gallo. Folkways paid a modest one-off fee and allowed Gallo rights in a few African territories, while Folkways gained the copyright everywhere else. "Because they agreed that they would pay Gallow a modest one-off fee, and let Gallow have the rights to the song in a few territories in Africa, and in return Folkways would get the copyright everywhere else."

podcast.title: Folk Music Promotion and Corporate Affiliation
podcast.body: Folkways was a record company specifically established to promote folk music, but it operated as part of a much larger conglomerate, the Richmond Organization. "Folkways, a company that was set up to promote Folk Music, but was part of a much bigger conglomerate, the Richmond organisation."

podcast.title: Initial Copyright of "Wimoweh"
podcast.body: When The Weavers decided to record "Wimoweh," Folkways contacted Gallo Records and was mistakenly informed that "Ember Bay" was a traditional song. Folkways then copyrighted "Ember Bay" as "Wimoweh" in the USA under the collective pseudonym Paul Campbell, preempting Gallo's later attempt to copyright it under Solomon Linda's name. "Folkways copyrighted Ember Bay as Wimmer Way, in the name Paul Campbell, a collective pseudonym that the Weevers used for their arrangements of traditional songs."

podcast.title: Released Harry Smith's Anthology
podcast.body: Folkways Records, owned by Moses Asch, collaborated with Harry Smith to release the groundbreaking "Anthology of American Folk Music" in 1952. "Smith and Merwash, the owner of Folkway's records, took advantage of the new medium, the long playing album, and put together a six album set of those recordings"
